::: {.callout-tip title="Who is this whitepaper for?"}
**Primary audience**: Senior developers, architects

**Prerequisites**: Claude Code experience (1+ month recommended)

**Reading time**: 25 min

**Key takeaways**:

- The agent loop proposes actions; the runtime applies permissions, hooks and execution controls
- 9 native tools and how to combine them effectively
- Model-dependent context budgets: inspect consumption before optimizing
:::

> **In 5 lines:** Understanding Claude Code's internal architecture changes how you use it. This whitepaper exposes the master loop (the fundamental reaction-action-observation cycle), the 9 native tools with their trade-offs, and the mechanics of model-dependent context budgets. With this mental model, you anticipate behaviors instead of reacting to them.

# Philosophy: Less Scaffolding, More Model

## Model and runtime responsibilities

A useful mental model is a loop: Claude receives context, proposes tool calls, observes results and continues. The runtime executes authorized tools and manages the session. This is a simplified description of observable behavior, not a complete account of private implementation.

Permissions, hooks, sandboxing, compaction and optional auto-mode classification all influence that loop. Plan mode, task tools, sub-agents and teams add ways to organize work. Their existence means that “only a loop, no planning or classifier” is not an accurate product description.

## Trade-offs

Model-driven tool selection can adapt to new evidence, but two runs can choose different sequences. Explicit instructions, tool scope and reproducible checks make the outcome easier to review. Evaluate a model with the same runtime configuration and task set; model quality alone does not establish a workflow's reliability.

Source: [How Claude Code works](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/how-claude-code-works).

## Current Models

Standard API rates, verified September 24, 2026. USD per million input/output tokens, excluding caching.

| Model | Input / output | Context | Default effort |
|-------|----------------|---------|----------------|
| Haiku 4.5 | $1 / $5 | 200K | Unsupported |
| Sonnet 5 | $2 / $10 | 1M | high |
| Opus 5.5 | $4 / $20 | 1M | medium |
| Fable 5.1 | $10 / $50 | 1M | high |

Sonnet's published rate remains $2/$10 after the launch promotion. Opus 5.5 is the direct-service default; account policy can override it. Model choice does not establish a typical task cost.

## Select and Save

`/model` opens the picker. **Enter** saves a default; **s** applies it to this session only. `claude --model sonnet` applies to the launched session. Project and managed settings can reapply at the next launch.

Aliases depend on the provider. `opus` maps to 5.5 on most providers, but 4.6 on Foundry. `sonnet` maps to 5 on the direct API, 4.6 on Claude Platform on AWS, and 4.5 on Bedrock, Google, and Foundry.

`fable` selects 5.1 where available, or 5 through the Claude apps gateway. `best` selects Fable when available, otherwise Opus. Pin a supported full ID when version identity matters.

## Thinking and Effort

Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5, and Fable 5.1 use adaptive thinking. Haiku 4.5 supports extended thinking but has **no effort parameter**.

Current adaptive models support `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, and `max`. Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 support `max` but not `xhigh`.

`/effort` saves levels through `xhigh` per model. Use **s** for a session-only choice. `max` is session-only; `/effort auto` clears the active model's saved choice.

`Option+T` / `Alt+T` toggles thinking where supported. It has no effect on Opus 5.5 or Fable, whose thinking is always enabled. Lower effort for bounded work instead.

`ultrathink` adds a reasoning instruction without changing API effort. `think hard` is ordinary prompt text.

## Choose by Measured Results

Evaluate Haiku on bounded tasks, Sonnet on routine work, and Opus or Fable on harder tasks. Compare accepted outcomes, retries, latency, and total cost on the same task set. Teammates can use different models.

Sources: [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config), [API pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing).

::: {.callout-warning title="Incident: Triple Harness Regression (March-April 2026)"}
Between March and April 2026, three independent harness changes simultaneously degraded Claude Code output quality, a 6-week regression before full resolution:

| Incident | Date | Impact | Resolution |
|----------|------|--------|------------|
| Default effort high → medium | March 4 | Shallower reasoning | Reverted April 7 (v2.1.116) |
| Thinking tokens cleared per turn | March 26 | Lost cross-turn context | Fixed April 10 (v2.1.101) |
| Verbosity system prompt added | April 16 | More verbose responses | Reverted April 20 (v2.1.116) |

**Architectural lesson**: harness parameters (default effort, thinking token management, system prompt) have a direct, measurable impact on perceived output quality, independent of the model. Diagnosing these regressions requires observability on configuration parameters, not just on outputs.

Source: Anthropic official postmortem + Boris Cherny HN comments, April 2026.
:::

# The Master Loop

## The Heart of Claude Code

A simplified teaching model of the agentic cycle is:

```
while (claude_response.has_tool_call):
    result = execute_tool(tool_call)
    claude_response = send_to_claude(result)
return claude_response.text
```

## Loop Visualization

```
  Your Prompt
      │
      v
  Claude reasons
  (Runtime controls still apply)
      │
      ├─── Tool needed ──→  Execute the tool
      │                          │
      │                     Result injected
      │                     into context
      │                          │
      │◄─────────────────────────┘
      │
      └─── No tool ──→  Text response (Done)
```

The loop can include planning and delegation. Proposed calls pass through the applicable permission, hook and sandbox checks before their results return to context. Task decomposition and stop conditions should be explicit when the workflow needs them.

## What This Means

The model itself decides:
- **When** to call a tool
- **Which** tool to call
- **When** it's done

The model proposes actions within the tools and controls supplied by the runtime.

::: {.callout-note title="Illustrative scenario: Marc, senior dev at a logistics SMB"}
Marc asks "add Zod validation to the shipping form". Claude enters the master loop: (1) Glob to find `ShippingForm.tsx`, (2) Read to understand the structure, (3) Grep to identify existing Zod imports, (4) Edit to add the validation schema, (5) Bash to run tests. This illustrative sequence contains five tool calls; it does not establish an exact count of inference requests.
:::

> 📖 **Read more:** [Architecture Internals](https://github.com/FlorianBruniaux/claude-code-ultimate-guide/blob/main/guide/core/architecture.md): master loop, tool arsenal, sub-agent architecture, edit tool internals

## Request Lifecycle

From the moment you type a command to the display of the result, here is the complete flow:

```
  Request Lifecycle

  1. User          →  Type command
  2. Claude Code   →  Load context (CLAUDE.md + history)
  3. Claude Code   →  Send prompt + full context  →  Claude API
  4. Claude API    →  Response + tool_use calls   →  Claude Code
  5. Claude Code   →  Execute tools (Read/Edit/Bash/Grep...)
  6. Local Tools   →  Tool results                →  Claude Code
  7. Claude Code   →  Return tool_results         →  Claude API
  8. Claude API    →  Final response (or new tool_use)  →  Claude Code
  9. Claude Code   →  Display result              →  User
```

Each round-trip to the Claude API consumes tokens (input + output). Tool calls, retries, auxiliary requests and caching affect total usage; an iteration count alone does not determine billed requests.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Native Tools

The master loop decides when to act; native tools are what it acts with. Each tool has a token cost and a precise scope. Understanding what each tool does (and costs) lets you calibrate expectations and diagnose slow sessions.

## Full Arsenal (9 main tools)

These 9 tools form the interface between the model's reasoning and the local filesystem. Each is specialized for a precise task, letting the model pick the most efficient tool rather than routing everything through Bash. The most recent addition (LSP Tool) was added to address a gap identified by the community in production usage; the batch-replace use case is covered by Edit's `replace_all: true` option, and multi-file operations go through the Agent tool (formerly Task) or scripted Bash.

| Tool | Purpose | Key Behavior |
|------|---------|--------------|
| **Bash** | Execute shell commands | Universal adapter |
| **Read** | Read file contents | Max 2000 lines |
| **Edit** | Modify existing files | Diff-based, exact match; `replace_all: true` to replace a pattern throughout the file |
| **Write** | Create/overwrite files | Must read first if exists |
| **Grep** | Search within files | ripgrep-based |
| **Glob** | Find files by pattern | Sorted by mtime |
| **Agent** (formerly Task) | Spawn sub-agents | Isolated context, 3 levels deep by default |
| **TodoWrite** | Track progress | Structured task management; disabled by default on Sonnet 5/Opus 4.8/Fable 5 and newer models since v2.1.233, re-enable with `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1` |
| **LSP Tool** (v2.0.74+) | Code intelligence | Symbols, references, diagnostics |

## Bash: The Universal Adapter

**Key insight**: Bash is Claude's Swiss army knife. It can:

- Execute any CLI (git, npm, docker, curl...)
- Run scripts
- Chain commands with pipes
- Access system state

The model was trained on massive amounts of shell data, making it highly effective at using Bash as a universal adapter.

## Tool Selection (Model-Driven)

```
"Read auth.ts"           → Read tool
"Find all test files"    → Glob tool
"Search for TODO"        → Grep tool
"Run npm test"           → Bash tool
"Explore the codebase"   → Agent tool (sub-agent)
"Track my progress"      → TodoWrite tool
```

The model learns these patterns during training. For dangerous patterns (rm -rf, sudo, etc.), explicit rules in the system prompt complement the training; see the Security section.

## Token Cost Per Tool

Every tool call consumes tokens from the context budget, in input (the request to the tool) and output (the result returned). These costs accumulate with each master loop iteration, making tool selection directly tied to session economics. A poorly targeted Read on a large file can consume as much as a dozen targeted Grep calls.

Tool costs depend on argument length, result size, prior context, caching and retries. Measure actual usage for a representative task rather than assigning a fixed token cost to Read, Edit or Agent. Targeted reads often reduce unnecessary context, but the result must still contain enough evidence to complete the task.

## Execution and retrieval

Independent tool operations may run concurrently where the runtime supports it. Scheduling and internal search binaries can change across versions; this whitepaper does not establish a universal concurrency limit or a measured speedup.

## Advanced API patterns

Programmatic tool calling, tool search and examples in tool definitions are separate API capabilities. Evaluate them against the current API documentation and your own task set before attributing a published benchmark gain to a Claude Code session.

# Context Management

## Context Budget (Model-Dependent)

> **Current windows**: Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5, and Fable 5.1 use native 1M context; Haiku 4.5 uses 200K. See the model table below.

```
  ILLUSTRATIVE 200K CONTEXT BUDGET
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  System Prompt         ~5-15K tokens│
  │  CLAUDE.md Files        ~1-10K tokens│
  │  Conversation History   variable    │
  │  Tool Results           variable    │
  │  Reserved for Response ~40-45K tokens│
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘
          │
          v
  USABLE = Total - System - Reserved
         ≈ 140-150K tokens
```

The context budget is a finite, non-extensible resource within a session. Every Read, every Bash, every Grep consumes space that will no longer be available for reasoning. This is why context management strategy directly conditions response quality toward the end of a session.


## Context Is Model-Specific

| Direct API model | Context | Maximum output |
|------------------|---------|----------------|
| Haiku 4.5 | 200K | 64K |
| Sonnet 5 | 1M native | 128K |
| Opus 5.5 | 1M native | 128K |
| Fable 5.1 | 1M native | 128K |

Verified September 24, 2026. Provider settings can expose different limits. Inspect `/context` for the active session.

## No Native-1M Premium

Current native 1M models use standard rates beyond 200K input tokens. They do not need the old long-context beta header. Sonnet 5 has no 200K variant on the direct API.

Older Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 have `[1m]` variants with plan/provider restrictions. Do not transfer their access rules to current models.

## Price a Complete Request

Illustrative USD totals without caching or retries:

| Input / output | Sonnet 5 | Opus 5.5 |
|----------------|----------|----------|
| 50K / 5K | $0.15 | $0.30 |
| 150K / 20K | $0.50 | $1.00 |
| 500K / 50K | $1.50 | $3.00 |

Use separate input, output, cache-read, and cache-write counts. A context-window size is capacity, not a bill or an accuracy score.

## Control Accumulation

`/context` shows the token breakdown. `/compact` summarizes the conversation; `/clear` starts fresh. Save decisions and verification commands before resetting context.

`/autocompact 500k` saves a smaller compaction window. `/autocompact auto` restores the model default. Native 1M sessions normally compact around 967K.

Load relevant files rather than filling the available window. Split independent tasks when separate contexts help. No fixed percentage guarantees reliable recall.

## Evaluate Retrieval

Older MRCR results for Opus 4.6 or Sonnet 4.5 remain results for those models and benchmark conditions. They do not establish retrieval quality for Sonnet 5 or Opus 5.5.

Test on your own document set with answerable questions, expected citations, and distractors. Measure missed evidence as well as correct answers.

Sources: [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config), [model specifications](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/overview), [pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing).

## Auto-Compaction

Auto-compaction depends on the model window and reserved capacity. Native 1M sessions normally compact around 967K tokens. `/autocompact 500k` chooses a smaller window; `/autocompact auto` restores the model default. Manual `/compact` remains available at a useful task boundary.

**What happens**:
1. Lightweight pre-compaction pass (micro-compaction): selectively compresses older tool results without touching conversation history
2. If insufficient: full compaction, older turns summarized, recent context preserved in full
3. "Context was compacted" signal sent to model

::: {.callout-tip title="📋 Memo: Context management"}
Inspect `/context`, keep the information needed for the task, and save decisions before compaction or handoff. Percentage thresholds can be personal reminders; they do not prove a loss of reasoning quality. Automatic compaction depends on the active model and configuration.
:::

If Claude repeats reads, loses a constraint or proposes an unsupported path, check the current evidence and reopen the relevant files. These symptoms have multiple possible causes and cannot be diagnosed from context percentage alone.

## The /context Command (v2.1.15+)

Analyzes the current context window contents:

```bash
/context
```

**Illustrative output for a 200K session**:
```
Token breakdown:
  System prompt:        12,450 tokens (6.2%)
  CLAUDE.md files:      3,200 tokens (1.6%)
  Conversation:         45,300 tokens (22.6%)
  Tool results:         89,150 tokens (44.5%)
  Available:            50,000 tokens (25.1%)

Recent large tool results:
  Read src/auth.ts:     8,920 tokens
  Bash npm test:        12,430 tokens
  Grep search:          5,680 tokens
```

**Use case**: Diagnose why context fills up fast, identify massive tool results.

## Decision Tree: Which Mechanism to Activate?

```
  Need to access an external resource?
  │
  ├─ Yes → API/DB/Browser?
  │         ├─ Yes → MCP Server (Context7, Serena, etc.)
  │         └─ No  → Local semantic search?
  │                   ├─ Yes → Grepai (Layer 4, local)
  │                   └─ No  → Parallelizable task or isolation needed?
  │                             ├─ Yes → Agent Tool / Agent Teams
  │                             └─ No  → Native Tools (Bash, Read, Edit...)
  │
  └─ No  → Validate or log actions?
            ├─ Yes → Hooks (PreToolUse/PostToolUse)
            └─ No  → Workflow repeated multiple times?
                      ├─ Yes → User-invocable Skill (.claude/skills/, disable-model-invocation: true)
                      └─ No  → Native Tools (sufficient)
```

## Context Engineering: Mental Model

Claude Code = 4 hierarchical context layers:

```
  Layer 1: System Prompt     (runtime supplied)
      │
      v
  Layer 2: Instructions      (scope dependent)
      │
      v
  Layer 3: Session           (variable)
      │
      v
  Layer 4: External Memory   (Outside context window)
```

You control applicable instruction files, while system instructions and loaded context can change with the runtime and configuration. Layer 3 is the volatile zone; that's where optimization matters most. Layer 4 lets you offload storage outside the context window, preserving space for reasoning.

**Effective strategy**: Keep relevant session evidence, concise instructions and scoped external retrieval; maximizing any layer blindly can add noise or risk.

### Layer 3 in Action: cc-sessions (Composable Session History)

**cc-sessions** illustrates a key Claude Code architectural principle: the JSONL storage in `~/.claude/projects/` is not accidental. It makes session history *composable*: queryable by script, filterable by date/branch, resumable by third-party tools.

| Capability | Mechanism |
|-----------|-----------|
| Keyword search | Incremental JSONL index; latency depends on the history |
| Date/branch filters | `--since 7d`, `--branch develop` |
| Partial ID resume | `cc-sessions resume 8d472d` → `claude --resume <full-id>` |
| JSON output | Pipe to `jq`/`fzf` for advanced workflows |

```bash
# Search all "auth" sessions on main branch from the past week
cc-sessions search "auth" --since 7d --branch main

# Resume a session by partial ID
cc-sessions resume 8d472d
```

**Architectural principle**: Claude Code externalizes persistence as JSONL rather than a database; this deliberate choice allows tools like cc-sessions to index, filter, and compose session history with zero dependencies. That's Layer 3 made toolable.

→ **Download**: [examples/scripts/cc-sessions.py](https://github.com/FlorianBruniaux/claude-code-ultimate-guide/blob/main/examples/scripts/cc-sessions.py)

### Layer 4 in Action: Grepai (Local Semantic Search, v3.27.1)

**Grepai** is a concrete example of Layer 4: it operates entirely outside the context window (local indexing with Ollama + nomic-embed-text; returned excerpts can enter the model context) and replaces token-expensive Grep+Read patterns. → See also the **MCP Integration** section for other Layer 4 tools.

Compare returned context size, retrieval accuracy and completed-task cost on the same searches. No measured 15K-to-4K token reduction is established here.

```bash
# Search by intent (not by regex)
grepai_search("payment flow")      # Finds the payment flow
grepai_trace_callers("authenticate") # Who calls authenticate?
grepai_trace_graph("processOrder") # Full call graph
```

**"Less Scaffolding" alignment**: Grepai does local RAG without infrastructure; the model reasons on relevant snippets, not the entire file.

> 📖 **Read more:** [§2.2 Context Management](https://github.com/FlorianBruniaux/claude-code-ultimate-guide/blob/main/guide/ultimate-guide.md#22-context-management): context zones, compaction strategies, /compact vs auto-compact

## Agent Memory (MEMORY.md)

Main-session auto-memory is enabled by default and stored under `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/`. Its `MEMORY.md` index loads up to 200 lines or 25KB, whichever limit comes first; supporting files can be read when needed. Inspect or configure it with `/memory`.

Custom agents have a separate `memory` field:

| Scope | Path |
|-------|------|
| `user` | `~/.claude/agent-memory/<agent>/` |
| `project` | `.claude/agent-memory/<agent>/` |
| `local` | `.claude/agent-memory-local/<agent>/` |

Enabling agent memory adds Read, Write and Edit tools. Omit it when the agent must remain strictly read-only. Review persistent content before sharing it.

# Sub-Agents: The Agent Tool

Native tools operate within the main agent's context. But certain tasks (broad exploration, parallel search, risky analysis) benefit from isolated context. That's the role of the Agent tool (formerly named Task): spawn a sub-agent with its own context window, which returns a summary without polluting the main context.

## Isolation Architecture

```
  Isolation Architecture

  1. Main Agent      →  Sub-Agent (level 1)  : Agent("Explore authentication patterns")
                                                [Fresh context | Same tools except Agent]
  2. Sub-Agent (n1)  →  Sub-Agent (level 2)  : Agent("Deep-dive OAuth flow")
                                                [3 levels deep by default]
  3. Sub-Agent (n2)  →  Sub-Agent (n2)       : Glob, Read, Grep...
  4. Sub-Agent (n2)  →  Sub-Agent (n1)       : Summary text only
  5. Sub-Agent (n1)  →  Main Agent           : Summary text only
                                                (Only each level's summary bubbles up)
```

Ordinary sub-agents start with their prompt and applicable configuration rather than the complete parent transcript. Supported forked workflows can inherit context. The parent normally receives the result or summary; its size varies and errors can propagate through it.

## Why a Depth Limit of 3 Levels?

Since v2.1.172 (June 2026), a sub-agent can spawn its own sub-agents; v2.1.172 initially raised that cap to five levels. v2.1.217 reverted this and disabled nesting entirely (depth back to 1), adding `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS` to cap concurrency along the way. v2.1.219 restored nesting to a default depth of 3, the value still in effect; set `CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH=1` to disable nesting and return to the strict single-level behavior. The 3-level cap serves the same goal as the old hard limit, containing the risk of runaway recursion, while unlocking real use cases like recursively decomposing a broad exploration (an architecture agent that delegates each subsystem to a dedicated agent, which in turn delegates each module).

| Risk | Explanation | What the 3-level cap changes |
|------|-------------|-------------------------------|
| Recursive explosion | Agent-ception would consume infinite resources | The hard cap prevents unbounded chains, but three levels is still enough to trigger a combinatorial explosion if each level spawns several children in parallel |
| Context pollution | Each level would accumulate context | Still true: only the summary bubbles up at each level, isolation protects the parent even on a deep chain |
| Debugging nightmare | Tracing multi-level chains is hard | The risk grows with depth; tracing a 3-level chain needs observability Claude Code doesn't yet expose in fine detail |
| Unpredictable costs | Nested agents = unpredictable tokens | Budget becomes harder to estimate upfront; in practice most tasks stay useful at 2 levels, beyond that the ROI drops fast |

## Sub-Agent Types

| Type | Purpose | Available Tools |
|------|---------|----------------|
| `Explore` | Codebase exploration | All read-only |
| `Plan` | Architecture planning | All except Edit/Write |
| `Bash` | Command execution | Bash only |
| `general-purpose` | Complex multi-step | All tools |

## When to Use Sub-Agents

| Use Case | Why Sub-Agent Helps |
|----------|---------------------|
| Large codebase search | Keeps main context clean |
| Parallel exploration | Multiple simultaneous searches |
| Risky exploration | Exploration stays separate; verify returned findings |
| Specialized analysis | Different "mindset" per task |

::: {.callout-note title="Illustrative scenario: Leila, lead dev at a fintech"}
Leila is debugging a performance issue on the payment API. Rather than reading all 12 involved files in the main context, she launches three sub-agents in parallel: one explores Express routes, one analyzes Prisma queries, one checks authentication middleware. Each sub-agent returns a 500-token summary. Result: 1500 tokens in the main context instead of ~30K if she had read everything directly.
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Agent Teams: Autonomous Coordination

**Status**: Experimental (v2.1.32+, models selected per teammate)

Sub-agents can run in the foreground or background. For tasks requiring real coordination between multiple autonomous agents (each with its own 1M-token context window), Agent Teams represent the next step.

## Lead-Teammate Architecture

```
  Lead-Teammate Architecture

  Team Lead (Main session)
      │
      ├─── spawn ──→  Teammate 1 (own context)
      │                    │
      │                    ├─────────────────────────┐
      │               peer-to-peer mailbox            │
      │                    │                          │
      └─── spawn ──→  Teammate 2 (own context) ◄────────┘
      │
      └─── coordination ──→  Shared task claims
                             Mailbox messages
```

**Key capabilities**:
- Isolated context per agent, sized by its model
- Peer-to-peer communication via mailbox (not just hierarchical)
- Shared task coordination; file locking prevents duplicate claims, not source conflicts
- Solution debate between agents (challenge approaches)

## Activation

```bash
export CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1
claude
```

Or in `~/.claude/settings.json`:
```json
{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS": "1"
  }
}
```

## Validated Use Cases

**Read-heavy tasks** (Excellent):
- Multi-layer code review (security + API + frontend)
- Parallel hypothesis testing (3 root causes → 3 agents)
- Architecture analysis (explore alternatives)

**Write-heavy tasks** (Risky):
- Refactoring shared files → merge conflicts
- Coordinated migrations → timing issues

## When to Use

| Criteria | Teams | Single |
|----------|-------|--------|
| Complexity | >5 files, multi-layers | <5 files |
| Type | Read-heavy (analysis) | Write-heavy (edits) |
| Budget | Measure parallel usage and coordination cost | Measure sequential accepted-task cost |
| Coordination | Shared tasks and messages | One execution context |

Claims about workforce screening or feature delivery in other deployments are not benchmarks of Claude Code Agent Teams. Measure the specific workflow you intend to use.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Background Agents: Async Tasks

**Introduced**: v2.0.60 | **Status**: Stable

## Concept

Agents that execute in the background without blocking the main session.

**Use cases**:
- Long test suites (>5min)
- CI/CD builds
- Database migrations
- Long-running scripts

## Background Launch

Ask Claude to run an appropriate task in the background, or use `Ctrl+B` for a running task where supported. Inspect `/tasks` to see its progress and result. A prompt beginning with `&` requests a cloud task on supported accounts; it is not the generic local-background syntax.

Both foreground and background execution can use the Agent tool. Choose based on whether the main task can continue independently.

## Architecture

```
  Background Agent Architecture

  Main session (keeps working)
      │
      └─── spawn async ──→  Background Agent
                                 │
                                 v
                            Execute the task
                                 │
                                 v
                            Log progress
                                 │
                                 v
                            Notification when done
                                 │
                                 └── summary (async) ──→  Main session
```

**Context**: Do not assume every background agent inherits the complete session. Forked context and ordinary sub-agent delegation have different contracts.

**Monitoring**:
```bash
/tasks                   # Inspect running tasks and their results
```

## When to Use Background

| Scenario | Background | Synchronous |
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| Tests >5min | Yes | No (blocks session) |
| Heavy builds | Yes | No (context overflow) |
| DB migrations | Yes | No (pointless waiting) |
| Quick feature | No (overhead) | Yes (direct) |

## Worktrees and Branch Isolation

Git worktrees let you run Claude Code in an isolated branch without affecting your current workspace. Useful for testing risky changes or parallelizing tasks.

```bash
claude --worktree              # Create a worktree from the remote branch
# To branch from local HEAD, configure worktree.baseRef as shown below
```

> **Breaking change (v2.1.133)**: `worktree.baseRef` now defaults to `fresh` (from remote `origin/<default-branch>`), reverting the v2.1.128 behavior where worktrees branched from local HEAD. If you have unpushed commits to include in the worktree, set `"worktree": {"baseRef": "head"}` explicitly in `settings.json`.

```json
{
  "worktree": {
    "baseRef": "head"
  }
}
```

| Value | Behavior |
|-------|----------|
| `fresh` (default) | Branch from `origin/<default-branch>`, always a clean remote base |
| `head` | Branch from local HEAD, includes unpushed commits |

{{< pagebreak >}}

# MCP Integration

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) extends Claude Code's capabilities beyond its native tools. Where native tools cover file and shell operations, MCP lets you connect specialized external servers (documentation, semantic search, browser automation) without modifying Claude Code's core.

## How MCP Works

```
  CLAUDE CODE
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Native Tools                           │
  │  Bash, Read, Edit...                    │
  │                                         │
  │  MCP Tools                              │
  │  mcp__serena__*                         │
  │  mcp__context7__*     ──→  JSON-RPC 2.0 │──→  MCP SERVER
  │  mcp__custom__*                         │     stdio/HTTP transport
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘     Tool definitions
                                                   Implementations
```

The model treats MCP tools exactly like native tools: it proposes calls through the connected server and the applicable permission checks. Transport, server implementation and access controls determine what the server can do.

## Key MCP Facts

The MCP protocol rests on a few simple principles that shape how it works in practice. The MCP server only receives call parameters, not the full conversation context, but that protocol boundary is not filesystem or process isolation. A local server may be able to access files or network services using its own credentials.

| Aspect | Behavior |
|--------|----------|
| Protocol | JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio or HTTP |
| Tool naming | Convention `mcp__<server>__<tool>` |
| Context sharing | Via parameters and return values only |
| Lifecycle | Depends on connection type, configuration and runtime |
| Permissions | Same system as native tools |

## MCP security boundaries

A tool request does not automatically include the full conversation, but a server can retain state, read resources available to its process, and return malicious instructions in metadata or results. Review its implementation and requested access. Permission approval for one tool is not a guarantee that the server is harmless.

## Extension Mechanisms Comparison

Claude Code offers 4 ways to extend its behavior, with very different profiles:

| Mechanism | Complexity | Added Latency | Persistence | Typical Use Case |
|-----------|-----------|---------------|-------------|------------------|
| **Hooks** | Low | Script dependent | Session | Validation, logging, command blocking |
| **MCP** | Medium | Server dependent | Configurable | External APIs, DB, browser |
| **Skills** | Low | None | Global | Recurring workflows (user-invocable) + knowledge modules (model-invocable) |
| **Agents** | High | Variable | Session | Parallel tasks, multi-file analysis |

**Selection rule**: Hooks to intercept, MCP to access, Skills to automate, Agents to parallelize.

::: {.callout-note title="Hooks → MCP Tools (v2.1.118)"}
Since v2.1.118, hooks can invoke MCP tools directly via `type: "mcp_tool"` in hook configuration. This creates a new architectural extension point: hooks are no longer limited to shell scripts, they can call tools on an already-connected MCP server.

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "hooks": [{
        "type": "mcp_tool",
        "server": "my-mcp-server",
        "tool": "log_tool_call"
      }]
    }]
  }
}
```

Impact: hooks become an integration bus between Claude Code and the MCP ecosystem, enabling real-time observability, automated auditing, and cross-tool validation.
:::

> 📖 **Read more:** [§8 MCP Servers](https://github.com/FlorianBruniaux/claude-code-ultimate-guide/blob/main/guide/ultimate-guide.md#8-mcp-servers): configuration, selection, security | [MCP Ecosystem](https://github.com/FlorianBruniaux/claude-code-ultimate-guide/blob/main/guide/ecosystem/mcp-servers-ecosystem.md)

{{< pagebreak >}}

# The Security Model

The model-driven loop runs within a configurable execution environment. On the contrary, the permission model is structured in 4 progressive layers, from the simplest user interaction to full filesystem isolation.

## The 4 Permission Layers

```
  Layer 1: INTERACTIVE PROMPTS
           Allow once | Allow always | Deny | Edit
                │
                v
  Layer 2: ALLOW/DENY RULES
           settings.json
                │
                v
  Layer 3: HOOKS
           PreToolUse | PostToolUse
                │
                v
  Layer 4: SANDBOX
           Filesystem isolation + network
```

Each layer is independent and cumulative. Layer 1 is sufficient for personal use. Layers 2-3 are recommended for teams. Layer 4 is intended for CI/CD environments and automated pipelines where no human supervises execution.

## Dangerous Patterns Detected

The model learns to recognize destructive commands during training, but that alone is insufficient for a production system. Explicit rules in the system prompt complement this learning alongside runtime permission controls. Prompt behavior depends on mode, rules, hooks and sandbox configuration.

| Pattern | Risk | Behavior |
|---------|------|----------|
| `rm -rf` | Destructive deletion | Depends on active controls |
| `sudo` | Privilege escalation | Depends on active controls |
| `curl \| sh` | Remote code execution | Depends on active controls |
| `chmod 777` | Insecure permissions | Depends on active controls |
| `git push --force` | History destruction | Depends on active controls |
| `DROP TABLE` | Data destruction | Depends on active controls |

These patterns are detected via model training AND explicit rules in the system prompt.

::: {.callout-tip title="📋 Memo: Quick Security Reference"}
**What**: 4 permission layers (prompts, rules, hooks, sandbox).

**When**: Prompts = personal use. Rules + Hooks = team. Sandbox = CI/CD.

**How**: `settings.json` for rules, `.claude/hooks/` for hooks.

**Verify**: Run `/permissions` inside an interactive Claude Code session to inspect active rules.
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

# How the Edit Tool Works

Edit replaces specified text in an existing file. Supply current content and enough surrounding text to identify the intended occurrence. Private matching fallbacks are not a stable public contract; re-read the file after another process or agent changes it.

## Edit Validation

| Check | Purpose |
|-------|---------|
| File exists | Prevent creation via Edit |
| old_string found | Ensure editing the right place |
| Single match | old_string must be unique |
| New content differs | Prevent no-op edits |

## When Edit Fails

| Error | Cause | Claude's Response |
|-------|-------|-------------------|
| "old_string not found" | Content changed since last read | Re-reads file, retries |
| "Multiple matches" | old_string not unique | Uses more context |
| "File not found" | Wrong path | Searches for correct path |

::: {.callout-note title="Illustrative scenario: Antoine, junior dev at a SaaS startup"}
Antoine notices that Claude fails to edit a file with "old_string not found". Reading the logs, he realizes another tool (Bash with prettier) reformatted the file between the Read and the Edit. The content changed, the exact match fails. Solution: in his CLAUDE.md, Antoine adds a rule "always re-read a file before editing it if more than 2 tool calls separate the Read from the Edit".
:::

# Claude Code vs Alternatives

## Compare workflows on current evidence

Products and integrations change quickly. Evaluate terminal and IDE workflows, cloud execution, supported models, MCP access, permission controls and traceability against the current product documentation. Historical Copilot Workspace previews and older Cursor feature tables are not a reliable current comparison.

Choose a representative task, fix the model and configuration where possible, and compare the accepted result, latency, review effort and total cost. Claude Code offers terminal workflows and editor integrations; test the surface your team actually uses.

## Four Layers, Four Responsibilities

Comparing products only by model or interface hides the responsibility that matters: who decides the next action. The [harness selection guide](https://cc.bruniaux.com/guide/agent-harness-landscape/) separates four layers.

| Layer | Responsibility | What it does not decide |
|-------|----------------|--------------------------|
| Model | Proposes text and tool calls | Permission or task recovery |
| Runtime harness | Runs the loop, calls tools, observes, and selects the next turn | Repository-specific conventions |
| Repository harness | Supplies project instructions, task state, and verification | The runtime inference loop |
| Orchestrator | Distributes work across runtimes or sessions | The detailed behavior of each runtime |

An orchestrator can launch several harnesses without becoming their runtime. Conversely, a repository can strengthen its instructions and controls without changing runtime. The distinction localizes a failure: loop and permissions at the runtime layer, change contract at the repository layer, coordination at the orchestrator layer. See also [Agent Harness Engineering](https://cc.bruniaux.com/guide/agent-harness/) and the [glossary](https://cc.bruniaux.com/guide/glossary/).

# Resources

## What We DON'T Know

Despite Anthropic's growing transparency, several internal aspects of Claude Code remain publicly undocumented. These blind spots do not prevent effective use of Claude Code, but they limit the ability to fine-tune sessions or predict certain behaviors.

| Topic | Status |
|-------|--------|
| Compaction threshold | Model/configuration dependent; inspect `/context` and `/autocompact` |
| System prompt contents | Not public, varies by version |
| Token counting method | Exact tokenizer, overhead |
| Model fallback | Does Claude Code fall back? |
| Internal caching | Is there caching between sessions? |

**Model knowledge cutoffs** (official):

| Model | Knowledge Cutoff |
|-------|-----------------|
| Sonnet 5 | January 2026 |
| Opus 5.5 | June 2026 |
| Fable 5.1 | June 2026 |
| Sonnet 4.6 | August 2025 |
| Opus 4.6 | May 2025 |
